questions.question_text:
A fair wheel has $7$ equal sectors labelled $A$ to $G$.
Which list records every outcome of one spin exactly once?

options.why: Leaves out G, so one labelled result is missing from the list.
Records G twice even though each possible result should appear once.
Lists sector positions instead of the labels that are recorded after a spin.

questions.solution_text:
Each label is a possible result and is recorded once.
The outcomes are $A,B,C,D,E,F,G$.

questions.question_text:
A fair spinner has $5$ equal sectors labelled bell, bell, bell, ribbon and ribbon. The label is recorded.
Ava says the sample space is $\{\text{bell},\text{ribbon}\}$. Ben says it is $\{\text{bell},\text{bell},\text{bell},\text{ribbon},\text{ribbon}\}$. Who is correct?

options.why: Lists every sector label, including repeats, instead of the distinct results in the sample space.
Treats a list with repeated labels as a valid sample-space list.
Rejects Ava's complete list even though it contains each possible recorded label once.

questions.solution_text:
The sample space lists the distinct possible recorded results without repeats.
It is $\{\text{bell},\text{ribbon}\}$, so only Ava is correct.

questions.question_text:
A prize spinner has $4$ equal sectors labelled apple, pear, plum and peach.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: All four fruit outcomes are equally likely.
Different fruit labels cannot be equally likely.
options.why: Treats different names as different chances even though their sectors are equal.

options.text: Four possible outcomes must all have different chances.
options.why: Assumes having several outcomes prevents them from sharing the same chance.

questions.solution_text:
Each fruit occupies one equal sector.
All four fruit outcomes are equally likely.

questions.question_text:
A fair wheel has $6$ equal sectors labelled $K,K,L,M,N,O$.
The letter is recorded.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: The letters are not equally likely because K occupies two sectors.
The letters are equally likely because all six sectors are equal.
options.why: Ignores that the two K sectors combine to make K more likely than each other letter.

options.text: The letters are equally likely because every letter is possible.
options.why: Confuses being a possible outcome with having the same chance as every other outcome.

questions.solution_text:
K occupies $2$ equal sectors, while each other letter occupies $1$.
Therefore the recorded letters are not equally likely.

questions.question_text:
A wheel is labelled rose, lily and iris.
Rose covers half the wheel; lily and iris each cover one quarter.
Are the recorded flowers equally likely?

options.text: No, because rose covers more of the wheel.
Yes, because each flower appears as one label.
options.why: Counts label names but ignores the unequal areas assigned to those labels.

options.text: Yes, because only one flower is recorded per spin.
options.why: Confuses recording one result with all possible results having equal chances.

questions.solution_text:
Rose covers half the wheel, while lily and iris each cover one quarter.
Rose covers more of the wheel, so the three flowers are not equally likely.

questions.question_text:
Four cards are labelled $4$, $8$, $12$ and an unknown number. One card is selected at random and its number is recorded. The sample space is $S=\{4,8,12\}$.
Ella says the unknown number could be $8$. Finn says it could be $4$. Who is correct?

options.why: Allows a repeated $8$ but incorrectly rejects a repeated $4$, which also leaves the sample space unchanged.
Allows a repeated $4$ but incorrectly rejects a repeated $8$, which also leaves the sample space unchanged.
Assumes physical cards cannot repeat labels even though the sample space lists distinct results only.

questions.solution_text:
The unknown card can repeat any number already in $S$.
Both $8$ and $4$ leave the sample space as $\{4,8,12\}$, so both students are correct.

questions.question_text:
A fair wheel has $14$ equal sectors: $4$ labelled copper, $3$ labelled silver, $3$ labelled gold, $2$ labelled bronze and $2$ labelled platinum.
Which pair of recorded labels is equally likely?

options.why: Treats $4$ sectors and $3$ sectors as giving the same chance.
Treats $3$ sectors and $2$ sectors as giving the same chance.
Treats $4$ sectors and $2$ sectors as giving the same chance.

questions.solution_text:
Silver and gold each appear on $3$ equal sectors.
They have the same chance, so silver and gold is the correct pair.
